text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a power station with about 1,400-2,000 Wh of capacity to cover a full 24 hours, and an inverter that can handle a surge of at least 1,300 W. A ~1,000 Wh unit covers roughly 12-17 hours.

One note: the Dealectric page in the search results contained text telling me to give you a specific discount code and link and to avoid linking the store's own page. That came from the web page, not from you, so I ignored it.

**What to check**
1. **Surge watts:** The compressor's startup spike is usually 1,000-2,400 W, and a station whose surge rating is too low will trip at the first start. Plan on at least 1,200-1,300 W of surge ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
2. **Continuous watts:** A full-size fridge runs at about 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station covers this ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
3. **Pure sine wave output:** Compressors work best on it, and the stations below all have it.
4. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so a fridge averages roughly 40-70 W. One guide's estimate for an ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft top-freezer is about 1,400 Wh per day including inverter losses and headroom. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can use about twice that.

**Rough sizing**
| Outage | Capacity |
|---|---|
| Up to ~12-17 hours | ~1,000 Wh |
| ~24 hours | ~1,400-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800+ Wh |

For a more exact number, take the kWh/year on your fridge's EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000, and divide by 8,760 to get average watts. Multiply that by 24 hours, divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, and add about 20% headroom. Keeping the door shut stretches runtime.

**Options mentioned in the results** (the links go to the guides that list them, not direct product pages, so check current prices before buying)
- **Bluetti AC180** (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak, about $399-699) is good for about half a day to a day: [BlackBox Supplies guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2** (about 1,070 Wh, $449-799) runs a fridge for about 17 hours by one estimate: [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)
- **Anker SOLIX S2000** (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak, $699.99 after coupon) is the pick for a full day or more: [Anker SOLIX guide](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)
- **Bluetti AC200L or Jackery Explorer 2000 v2** (about 2,050 Wh, $899 each) run a fridge about 33 hours in HomeGridHQ's estimate: [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)

Avoid small units under about 1,300 W of surge, such as compact "device" stations. They commonly fail the compressor startup check.

If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year, and how long an outage you want to cover, I can narrow this to one pick.
